title: The World's Oldest Temple Had a 12,000-Year-Old Bone Mystery –Two Graves Found at Göbekli Tepe May Have Finally Solved It

content:
Two intact graves excavated at Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Türkiye, appear to explain one of the site's oldest puzzles: why hundreds of loose human bone fragments have turned up mixed into the fill of its monumental buildings since digging began three decades ago.

Archaeologists have spent thirty years puzzling over an unusually grim detail at Göbekli Tepe, the roughly 11,600-year-old site often called the world’s oldest temple. Since excavations began in 1995, diggers have pulled more than 900 individual fragments of human bone out of the earthen fill packed into and around its monumental stone buildings — skull pieces mostly, scattered with no obvious pattern, never forming a complete skeleton.

A new study published in PLOS One by researchers Julia Gresky and Lee Clare offers what looks like the most convincing explanation yet: the fragments probably aren’t the remnants of some unknown funerary ritual at all. They’re what’s left of ordinary burials that once sat intact in the higher, older parts of the site — until landslides tore them apart and carried the pieces downhill into the fill of buildings below.

The case rests on two burials the team excavated at the site and describes in full for the first time: the first complete, undisturbed graves ever found at Göbekli Tepe.

A UNESCO site with a very old, very public mystery

Göbekli Tepe sits about 9 miles (15 km) northeast of the modern city of Şanlıurfa, in southeastern Türkiye. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2018, and it’s widely regarded as one of the most important archaeological finds of the past century — the site that pushed back, by thousands of years, what archaeologists thought hunter-gatherers were capable of building. Its T-shaped stone pillars, some carved with wild animals, are older than Stonehenge by roughly 6,000 years and the Egyptian pyramids by around 7,000.

The mound itself is artificial, built up over some 1,600 years, spanning the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A period, or PPNA (roughly 11,600 to 10,700 years ago), through the early and middle Pre-Pottery Neolithic B, or PPNB (about 10,700 to 10,000 years ago) — archaeological shorthand for the two phases of the Neolithic before pottery-making took hold in the region.

For the site’s first two decades of study, archaeologists read Göbekli Tepe as a purely ritual center, with no real evidence anyone had lived there. That view has shifted in recent years: excavators have found growing evidence of domestic life running through the whole sequence — the two burials at the center of this study among the clearest signs yet that people didn’t just visit the site. They lived, and were buried, there.

The bones that didn’t add up

Right from the start of excavation, workers kept finding human bone fragments in the fill of the special buildings and the spaces between them. Set the two new burials aside, and the tally stands at 928 individual fragments — mostly unconnected to one another, and bearing a set of taphonomic alterations: changes to bone that happen after death, whether from natural decay or deliberate human handling.

What made the pattern odd was its randomness. The fragments turned up scattered across every excavated layer of the site, spread over roughly 3,000 square meters (about 32,000 square feet, or three-quarters of an acre) — with no obvious concentration anywhere.

That raised an obvious question: had someone deliberately placed the bones there as part of some funerary practice archaeologists hadn’t documented before? Or had they simply ended up in the fill by accident?

Two competing theories

Researchers have floated two explanations for the scattered bones.

The first held that the fragments were deliberately placed there — a form of secondary or tertiary burial, where remains are moved or reprocessed some time after death. There was real evidence behind the idea. Skull fragments from what were originally three individuals — now five, with further finds — carry deep incisions cut along the midline of the skull, evidence of deliberate modification, possibly reserved for particular, important members of the community.

Cranial fragments also outnumbered the rest of the skeleton by a wide margin: 408 skull fragments against 283 from the rest of the body, hinting that whoever handled these remains may have been selecting skulls specifically.

That reading fit neatly with how archaeologists had already come to see Göbekli Tepe: a ritual center, its walls carved with headless human figures, stone heads separated from their bodies, and birds gripping severed human heads. Excavators have also found the bones of corvids — crows, ravens and their relatives, birds well known for scavenging — at roughly four times the rate seen at other sites from the same period nearby, a pattern some researchers have linked to open-air exhumation practices.

But the theory had a problem. At other sites from the same broader region and period — Karahantepe, Sefertepe, Çayönü Tepesi — skulls turn up in tight, localized clusters, exactly what you’d expect if people were placing them somewhere on purpose. At Göbekli Tepe, the fragments are spread everywhere, with skull pieces mixed in among fragments from the rest of the body, from both sexes and every age group. That’s not the pattern deliberate selection would produce.

The alternative: erosion, not ritual

The second theory points to something less dramatic: the bones came from ordinary, domestic burials that were disturbed and washed downhill by natural erosion. It leans on the same shift in how archaeologists now read the site — not a purely ceremonial complex, but a place where people actually lived, generation after generation.

The two burials at the heart of the new study both date to the early Pre-Pottery Neolithic B. One, in a trench designated DR1, sat beneath a plaster floor. The other, in trench L09-65, was probably under a floor too, though that layer has survived too poorly to say for certain. That second burial sits on the site’s western slope, above and overlooking what excavators call Special Building A — one of four such structures (A, B, C and D) that sit in a natural depression, hemmed in on three sides by accumulated debris from the mound above.

Burying the dead beneath the floors of ordinary rooms is a well-documented custom across the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, from Anatolia to the Levant — so finding it at Göbekli Tepe wasn’t a surprise. What was missing, until now, was an intact example.

What the two burials actually show

Excavators found the L09-65 burial in 2022, up against the eastern wall of a small room just west of Special Building A. The skeleton — a woman between 20 and 30 — had been laid on her left side in a flexed position, facing east, resting on a bed of fist-sized stones with no clearly cut grave pit beneath her.

The second burial, in trench DR1, came to light in 2017, during construction work on a drainage channel. Diggers found a kidney-shaped pit cut into the plaster floor of a rectangular Pre-Pottery Neolithic B building, containing the remains of at least three people — most of them out of anatomical order. Skulls had been placed in the pit’s southeast corner, other bones piled toward the center, with a few long bones laid along the western wall.

Three skulls and three jawbones, without any duplicate bones to suggest a fourth or fifth person, point to a minimum of three individuals: a woman at least 35 years old, a man between 20 and 30, and a teenage girl between 11 and 14. The researchers note a fourth person may also be represented among the remains.

What the bone damage reveals

Bones from both burials show heavy fragmentation after death. Between 70 and 100 percent of most fragment surfaces are coated in calcium carbonate deposits — the single most destructive force acting on bone at the site, since the mineral doesn’t just coat the surface but works its way into the bone itself, causing cracking and, eventually, breakage.

Most of the fractures have the jagged edges typical of ordinary postmortem breakage — the kind caused by the sheer weight of the soil above. But researchers also found smoother fracture edges and spiral breaks, the kind that only form while some collagen is still present in the bone — evidence some breakage happened relatively soon after burial.

Rodent gnaw marks turned up mainly on the bones of one individual. None of the bones show cut marks, heat damage, or traces of red ochre.

Putting the two lines of evidence together

The research team compared the damage on the two burials against the damage on the 928 loose fragments recovered from the special buildings’ fill over the decades — and found a close match: heavy fragmentation, extensive mineral crusting, and rodent gnawing, in both cases.

That matters most for the L09-65 burial, which is single, clearly undisturbed, and unambiguously a primary burial. The fact that its bones already carry the same damage as the scattered fragments strongly suggests that damage happened before anything moved — inside the burial itself, not afterward.

The most likely explanation, the authors argue, is that at least some of the human remains found inside the special buildings originally came from burials beneath the floors of buildings higher up the mound, later broken apart and carried downhill by erosion.

An open question, not a closed case

None of this rules out other funerary customs at Göbekli Tepe — the authors are careful to say so. The idea that people deliberately selected and placed human bones as part of some secondary or tertiary burial rite now looks less likely, but it hasn’t been ruled out entirely.

And the wider region tells a genuinely mixed story. At Sayburç, dated to the ninth millennium BC (roughly 11,000 years ago), excavators have found human bones tucked into wall niches, and in one case scattered across and in front of a stone bench inside a home. At Sefertepe, diggers have found a skull buried within the plaster of a niche floor, and at least 21 more packed into a small room researchers now call the “skull chamber.”

At Karahantepe, researchers have identified what looks like a distinct kind of secondary burial practice, marked by repeated incisions and burn damage on skulls — all of it part of the wider Taş Tepeler (“Stone Hills”) project, the cluster of Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in southeastern Türkiye that includes Göbekli Tepe.

The authors say what’s needed now is more osteological analysis and more absolute dating, to build a clearer chronological picture of how the people who built Göbekli Tepe actually treated their dead — and how that changed, if it changed at all, over the sixteen centuries the mound was in use.

A version of this article is also available in Spanish: Léelo en español
